edits.after:
### 4. **Wa qatilu al-mushrikina kaffatan**: The Clause That Gets Quoted at You

Then comes the clause this passage is most often quoted for, and it deserves more than a translation:

**wa qatilu al-mushrikina kaffatan kama yuqatilunakum kaffatan**.

And fight the polytheists all together, as they fight you all together.

[PAUSE]

Everything turns on one word: **kaffatan**. Here is what the classical commentaries say about it, one by one.

Al-Tabari explains the command like this: fight the polytheists, O believers, **jami'an** — all together, not divided; joined, not splintered — as the polytheists fight you all together, gathered and not scattered. For him the word describes the fighters' condition: the believers meeting as one undivided body an enemy that comes as one undivided body. He then records the early authorities saying the same thing in fewer words: al-Suddi — "**kaffah** means all, with your affair united"; Ibn 'Abbas — **jami'an**, all together; Qatadah — **jami'an**. He even adds a grammar note: **kaffah** never changes form, because it behaves like words such as *ma'an*, "together."

Ibn Kathir's short glosses run the same mirrored way: fight against the idolators collectively, "all of you," as they fight against you collectively, "all of them." Al-Muyassar writes simply: fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together. And al-Jalalayn also glosses the word **jami'an** — then adds a phrase of his own, "in all the months," which we will come back to.

[PAUSE]

Notice, second, that the command is not free-standing. It is indexed to something: **kama yuqatilunakum** — *as* they fight you. The same word, **kaffatan**, lands on both halves of the sentence. The believers' fighting is described in the mirror of the fighting already being brought against them. That reciprocity sits in the verse's own grammar before any commentator touches it.

And notice, third, where the clause lives. It does not float on its own. It sits inside a verse about the four sacred months, one breath after **fa-la tazlimu fihinna anfusakum**. Ibn Kathir reads it exactly there: he writes that initiating battle during the Sacred Months is forbidden, and that this clause "includes permission for the believers to fight the idolators in the Sacred Month, if the idolators initiate hostilities therein" — reciprocity again, this time governing sacred time. He reads it alongside 2:194, the sacred month for the sacred month, and 2:191, do not fight them at the Sacred Mosque unless they first fight you there. Al-Jalalayn's added phrase points a different way: for him the clause runs "in all the months." That is a real difference between these two editions — one keeps the sacred-month limits framing the clause, the other reads the clause across all months — and both deserve to be named rather than smoothed over.

None of this is a legal ruling, and none of it equips anyone to derive one. Rulings about war belong to qualified scholars and to those who carry public authority, not to a reflection like this one. What tadabbur can honestly do is what we have done here: read the words, report where the commentators stand, and refuse to let a clause built on *together* and *as* be quoted as though those two words were not in it.

### 5. **Innama al-nasi'u ziyadatun fi al-kufr**: Manipulating Sacred Time Is Not Neutral

Ibn Kathir (English): "(and fight against the idolators collectively), all of you, (as they fight against you collectively.), all of them" and "know that initiating battle during the Sacred Months is forbidden" and "it includes permission for the believers to fight the idolators in the Sacred Month, if the idolators initiate hostilities therein" (citing 2:194 and 2:191). al-Muyassar: "وقاتلوا المشركين جميعًا كما يقاتلونكم جميعًا". al-Jalalayn: "﴿وقاتلوا المشركين كافة﴾ جميعًا في كل الشهور".

edits.before: This is revealing. The passage does not simply ask how they behave while constrained. It asks how they would behave if power shifted. Character is often exposed most clearly by imagined or actual advantage.
edits.after: This is revealing. The passage does not simply ask how they behaved while constrained. It asks how they would have behaved if power shifted. Al-Muyassar reads the line against the record of that period: the way of those mushrikin was to hold to pacts only while others had the upper hand over them; once they sensed strength against the believers, they honored neither kinship nor treaty. And the editions know exactly which breach proved it. Ibn Kathir narrates it within this very passage: the Muslims kept the terms of the Hudaybiyyah treaty until Quraysh broke it, helping their allies Banu Bakr against Khuza'ah, the allies of Allah's Messenger — with some of Khuza'ah killed in the Sacred Area itself. Al-Jalalayn tells the same story in one line: the Prophet remained upright on their treaty until they broke it by aiding Banu Bakr against Khuza'ah. So the "if they gain the upper hand" of this verse was not an abstract psychology test. It had already been answered in events.

edits.before: The misranking itself is a form of zulm. It is an injustice in valuation.
edits.after: Who are "the wrongdoing people" here? The classical commentaries are specific, and they point in one direction: shirk. Al-Tabari records Ibn 'Abbas saying of the boasters, *fa-sammahumu Allahu zalimin bi-shirkihim* — "so Allah named them wrongdoers by their shirk" — and Ibn Kathir's edition carries the same explanation from Ibn 'Abbas: Allah described them with injustice on account of their shirk, and so their maintaining of the Masjid will not avail them. Al-Muyassar glosses the phrase as those who wrong themselves by kufr, and al-Jalalayn glosses *al-zalimin* in one word: the disbelievers. So the zulm this verse names is not, in these editions, a mistake of ranking. It is associating partners with Allah — which is exactly why the service, honorable as it looked, could not save the ones performing it. edits.after: Classical tafsir keeps the scene concrete. Ibn Kathir preserves the report of Abu Mas'ud, collected by al-Bukhari and Muslim: when the verses of charity came down, the Companions worked as porters to have something to give — a man came and distributed charity in abundance, and they said he was showing off; another man came with a single sa' of food, and they said Allah is not in need of this small amount. Al-Tabari's reports name the two ends of the donation line: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, who brought gold — forty uqiyyah in one report, a hundred in another — and Abu 'Aqil, who hauled water by rope through the night for two sa's of dates, kept one for his family, and brought the other.

edits.defect: (b)+(c) breadth defect: 'seventy = idiom' attributed to Ibn Kathir AND al-Tabari (al-Tabari's material runs the other way); false consensus over al-Jalalayn's recorded ikhtilaf
edits.before: As for **sab'ina marratan**, classical tafsir is very clear that seventy here is not an invitation to arithmetic experimentation. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari both preserve the Arab usage of such a number for emphatic abundance. The point is not that seventy-one might work. The point is that even multiplied intercession does not reverse a verdict rooted in chosen disbelief.
edits.after: As for **sab'ina marratan**, the commentaries do not speak with one voice about the number, and the honest version is more interesting than a smoothed one. Ibn Kathir carries the idiom reading: the seventy was mentioned to close the door on this subject, "for Arabs use this number when they exaggerate, not that they actually mean seventy." Al-Tabari's material runs the other direction: he preserves report after report — from 'Urwah, from Mujahid, from Qatadah, from Ibn 'Abbas — of the Prophet responding to this very verse by resolving to exceed the number, *la-azidanna 'ala sab'in*, "I will go beyond seventy," in hope that forgiveness might still be reached, until the verse of Surat al-Munafiqun (63:6) sealed the matter: whether you seek forgiveness for them or not, Allah will never forgive them. And al-Jalalayn sets both readings side by side as a recorded disagreement: it is said the seventy means emphatic abundance of istighfar, and it is said the specific number is meant — citing the Bukhari-collected words of the Prophet about going beyond it, "if I knew that were I to add beyond the seventy he would be forgiven, I would add to it," and "I will add beyond the seventy." Either way, the destination is the same, and it is the destination the verse cares about: multiplied intercession does not reverse a verdict rooted in chosen disbelief. The point is not that seventy-one might work. On Ibn Kathir's reading the number was never arithmetic; and on the reports al-Tabari and al-Jalalayn preserve, even the Prophet's resolve to exceed it was answered by a verse that closed the count entirely.
edits.evidence: Ibn Kathir: "The number seventy here was mentioned to close the door on this subject, for Arabs use this number when they exaggerate, not that they actually mean seventy or more than seventy." al-Tabari: "ويروى عن رسول الله ﷺ أنه حين نزلت هذه الآية قال: لأزيدنّ في الاستغفار لهم على سبعين مرة... فنزلت: ﴿سَوَاءٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أَسْتَغْفَرْتَ لَهُمْ أَمْ لَمْ تَسْتَغْفِرْ لَهُمْ لَنْ يَغْفِرَ اللَّهُ لَهُمْ﴾"; 'Urwah (17023): "لأزيدنّ على السبعين"; Mujahid (17025): "سأزيد على سبعين استغفارة"; Ibn 'Abbas (17030): "لأستغفرن أكثر من سبعين مرة"; Qatadah (17031): "فلأزيدنهم على سبعين". al-Jalalayn: "قِيلَ المُراد بِالسَّبْعِينَ المُبالَغَة فِي كَثْرَة الِاسْتِغْفار وفِي البُخارِيّ حَدِيث «لَوْ أعْلَم أنِّي لَوْ زِدْت عَلى السَّبْعِينَ غُفِرَ لَزِدْت عَلَيْها» وقِيلَ المُراد العَدَد المَخْصُوص لِحَدِيثِهِ أيْضًا «وسَأَزِيدُ عَلى السَّبْعِينَ» فَبَيَّنَ لَهُ حَسْم المَغْفِرَة بِآيَةِ ﴿سَواء عَلَيْهِمْ...﴾". The file's spiritual conclusion (no loophole at seventy-one) retained, grounded on Ibn Kathir's attribution alone plus the 63:6 sealing reports.
